# Siṅgāla Sutta (DN 31 (PTS DN iii 180))

**ID:** DN 31 (PTS DN iii 180)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Siṅgāla Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Advice to Sigālaka
**PTS:** DN iii 180
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn31
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Siṅgāla Sutta* (DN 31), also known as the *Sigālovāda Sutta* or *Sigālaka Sutta*, is the thirty-first discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Bodhi 2005; SuttaCentral]. Set near Rājagaha at the Bamboo Grove, the discourse takes place when the Buddha meets a young householder named Singālaka (or Sigālaka) who had risen early to worship the six cardinal directions in accordance with his deceased father's wishes [Buddhist Virtues in Socio-Economic Development 2011; SuttaCentral]. The Buddha reinterprets this ritual into a comprehensive code of moral discipline and social ethics for the laity, often described as "The Layperson's Code of Discipline" [Bodhi 2005; SuttaCentral]. Rather than performing external rites, the householder is instructed to honor reciprocal relationships across six social dimensions, including the fivefold mutual duties binding parents and children, teachers and pupils, and husbands and wives [Young 2004; Bodhi 2005]. The text combines prose instruction with stanzas introduced by traditional speech tags [Winternitz 1933; Anandajoti 2010].

The sutta forms part of an extensive cross-canonical textual cluster with at least thirteen distinct witnesses and fragments [Bingenheimer et al. 2013]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus identify full and partial parallels in Chinese Āgama literature—including the *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 16 / T 1, no. 16), the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 135 / T 26), and individual translations (T 16 and T 17)—as well as Central Asian Sanskrit fragments of the *Śikhālaka-sūtra* and citations in the *Mahākarmavibhaṅga* [Bingenheimer et al. 2013; SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments with Sanskrit and Tibetan texts (such as the *Ratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra* and *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*) and computes 1,485 Pali-internal reuse matches across 110 texts, showing dense textual overlap with canonical books (AN 3, AN 4, DN 16, MN 54) and commentaries such as the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].

In modern and traditional reception, the text has had significant educational and cultural influence. In 18th-century Myanmar, Singajā Sayardaw rendered its duties into popular mnemonic rhyming verses that remain a staple of primary schooling and moral instruction [Buddhist Virtues in Socio-Economic Development 2011]. Modern translations include those by Walpola Rahula, Nārada Thera, Bhikkhu Sujato, and the collaborative rendering by John Kelly, Sue Sawyer, and Victoria Yareham, as well as Japanese versions by Hajime Nakamura [Nakamura 1980; SuttaCentral; Than Hsiang Buddhist e-journal 2018].
